item.title: Drought Surcharge on Your Water Bill: What It Is and Why You
item.description:
Quick Answer

**A drought surcharge** is an extra fee water utilities add during dry periods to discourage high usage and cover increased supply costs. The fee is **tiered based on usage**—the more water you consume, especially outdoors, the higher the charge.

  • Drought surcharges add **$7-$76 per month** to your bill depending on usage tier
  • Example: Denver Water charges **$1.10 per 1,000 gallons** in Tier 2 and **$2.20 per 1,000 gallons** in Tier 3

Track your [monthly water usage](/blog/05-how-to-lower-utility-bills) to stay in lower tiers and reduce costs.

item.title: Why Did My Utility Bill Go Up This Month? (Even Without Using More)
item.description:
The short answer most people need

You open the bill, see a higher total, and think, "Nothing changed."

That feeling is common. Most increases come from a mix of billing days, rate changes, and fixed charges, not a sudden spike in usage.

If you want the broader map first, start with Utility Bills & Costs Explained. It shows how all the pieces fit together.

The three buckets that change your total

This part surprises a lot of people: your bill is not just usage. It is usage times price, plus fixed charges.

item.title: Water Service Charge Explained: What the Fixed Fee Covers (and Why You Still Pay It)
item.description:
The problem: your bill has a charge even when you used almost no water

You did not water the lawn. You were out of town. The usage on your bill looks tiny. And yet there it is: a water "service charge," "base charge," "customer charge," or "meter charge."

That moment is frustrating because it feels like you are paying for nothing.

You are not paying for "nothing," but you also should not have to guess what the fee means. This guide explains it in plain English and shows you how to sanity-check what you are being charged.

item.title: Electric Bill Breakdown: Every Charge Explained
item.description:
Quick Answer

Your electric bill contains 5-7 line items: Service Charge ($10-25 fixed), Energy Charge (usage × rate $0.08-0.15/kWh), Distribution/Transmission fees ($0.02-0.05/kWh), Regulatory/Environmental fees ($0.005-0.02/kWh), and Taxes (5-8%).

  • Fact: Delivery and transmission charges can add 30-50% on top of base energy costs
  • Action: Compare your “Energy Charge” month-over-month to track real usage changes vs. rate increases

For more detail, see How to Lower Your Electric Bill.

item.title: Why Your Utility Bill Can Be Higher Even If Your Usage Didn
item.description:
The short answer

A utility bill can be higher even when your "usage" looks similar because the total is not just usage x price. Most bills include a mix of: billing days, rate changes, fixed customer charges, and sometimes tiers or time-of-use pricing.

The fastest way to reduce confusion is to follow a simple order: days, usage per day, unit price, fixed fees, tiers.

For the overall billing model (usage vs delivery vs fixed fees), start at Utility Bills & Costs Explained.
